title: Heart Failure — Chronic to Acute
sources: Critical Vector — Heart Failure: Chronic to Acute (three-part continuum)
EMPEROR-Preserved NEJM 2021; DELIVER NEJM 2022; FINEARTS-HF NEJM 2024; STEP-HFpEF NEJM 2023
DanGer Shock (Møller JE et al. NEJM 2024;390:1382-1393) + 10-year follow-up (ESC 2025 / NEJM 2025)
ATTR-ACT (Maurer MS et al. NEJM 2018); EXPLORER-HCM (Lancet 2020); VALOR-HCM (JACC 2023)
SCAI SHOCK Stage Classification Expert Consensus Update. J Soc Cardiovasc Angiogr Interv 2022;1:100008

changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the CV three-part HF continuum: the six cardiomyopathy phenotypes, the HFpEF evidence scorecard + phenotype-driven treatment, and cardiogenic shock in the DanGer Shock era.

summary: One disease spectrum, three flashpoints: the cardiomyopathy phenotype underneath, the HFpEF syndrome that two unexpected drug classes finally cracked (SGLT2i, finerenone), and the cardiogenic shock event that still kills ~46% even with the device (Impella CP) proven to help.

rows: Globally dilated, hypokinetic LV, EF < 40%, not ischemic/valvular. Low voltage or LBBB. Titin (TTN) truncating variant is the commonest identifiable genetic cause
HFrEF GDMT (ARNI/ACE-I, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i). ICD if EF ≤ 35% after 3 mo optimized therapy; CRT if LBBB + QRS > 150 ms. Genetic testing if < 50 or family history
LV wall ≥ 15 mm (≥ 13 with family history) not explained by loading. LVOT gradient ≥ 30 mmHg = obstructive (oHCM)

Mavacamten (cardiac myosin inhibitor) for symptomatic NYHA II–III oHCM — REMS-restricted, boxed warning for systolic dysfunction, serial echo mandatory. VALOR-HCM: reduced need for septal reduction therapy
Epsilon wave V1–V3 (major criterion, ~29%), TWI V1–V4 (~88%), exercise-triggered VT, a 'normal-looking' echo early
2010 Revised Task Force Criteria. ICD for high SCD risk. AVOID competitive athletics (adrenergic trigger). Beta-blockers, antiarrhythmics, VT ablation
Apical ballooning with hyperdynamic base after emotional/physical stress; troponin disproportionately mild vs the wall-motion abnormality; ~90% postmenopausal women
Angiography to exclude true ACS FIRST — diagnosis of exclusion. Supportive (ACE-I / beta-blocker as tolerated); avoid inotropes if LVOT obstruction. Most recover in weeks
Low-voltage ECG despite echo LVH (the discordance is the clue); bilateral carpal tunnel history. Restrictive, non-dilated, thick-walled

PYP scan for ATTR; serum/urine free light chains + biopsy to exclude AL before treating as ATTR. Tafamidis — ATTR-ACT: 13.4% absolute all-cause mortality reduction; benefit greatest in NAC stage I/II — diagnose early
New systolic HF (EF < 45%) from the last month of pregnancy through 5 months postpartum, no other cause. Anti-angiogenic state (cleaved prolactin, sFlt-1)

Pregnancy/lactation-adapted GDMT. Bromocriptine (prolactin blockade) studied as a mechanism-targeted adjunct. Anticoagulate if very low EF. ~50% recover EF in 6–12 mo; recurrence risk with a subsequent pregnancy if EF has not normalized

body.text: > 50% of all heart failure, 20–29% one-year mortality, 21% 30-day readmission. Decades of negative trials (ACE-I/ARB — CHARM-Preserved, I-PRESERVE; sacubitril-valsartan — PARAGON-HF; spironolactone — TOPCAT missed its primary endpoint), then two unexpected drug classes worked.

rows: HR 0.79 (EMPEROR-Preserved) / 0.82 (DELIVER); meta-analysis n=21,947 HR 0.77 for CV death or HF hospitalization, NNT 25 over 23 mo. Works regardless of diabetes, across the full LVEF spectrum — Class I, start in all

HR 0.84, FINEARTS-HF 2024 — 16% reduction in worsening HF + CV death in LVEF ≥ 40%; lower hyperkalemia risk than spironolactone/eplerenone; separation from placebo within the first month; benefit consistent regardless of SGLT2i use
STEP-HFpEF, BMI ≥ 30 only — improved KCCQ, 6-min walk, NT-proBNP at 52 wks. QoL outcome, not yet mortality-reducing in HFpEF

items: Diagnosis (2023 ACC / 2021 ESC): LVEF ≥ 50% + HF signs/symptoms + a structural/functional abnormality (LVH, LA dilation, elevated filling pressures). NT-proBNP ≥ 125 pg/mL (SR) or ≥ 365 (AF). If uncertain: H2FPEF or HFA-PEFF (score ≥ 5/9 = high probability).

Phenotypes drive treatment — treating HFpEF as one disease is how the trials missed. Cardiometabolic/obese (~80%): SGLT2i + GLP-1 RA. Elderly hypertensive: BP < 130. AF phenotype: rhythm/rate control + anticoagulation. Amyloid phenotype (~13%): screen if LV wall ≥ 12 mm with low voltage.

SGLT2i is the universal first layer; finerenone, BP control, rhythm management, weight loss, and amyloid-specific therapy layer on top of the phenotype in front of you. Loop diuretics for congestion are indispensable but have no randomized mortality benefit — HFpEF patients are preload-dependent, over-diuresis causes low output and azotemia.

body.text: Part 3 — cardiogenic shock in the DanGer Shock era

rows: No CS signs/symptoms — large AMI or prior decompensated HF
Hypoperfusion requiring pharmacologic or mechanical support
Not responding to initial support — escalating therapy
Refractory circulatory collapse, often with arrest

body.text: The C → D jump (21.5% → 54.3% in-hospital) is the steepest cliff in the staging system — that's the window where escalation decisions matter most. SCAI-stage every patient A–E; the stage is the single strongest predictor in the room.

DanGer Shock (NEJM 2024, n≈360, STEMI + CS undergoing emergency PCI, 55% SCAI C): 180-day all-cause mortality 45.8% with Impella CP + standard care vs 58.5% standard care alone — HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.55–0.99), NNT 8. First RCT to prove an MCS survival benefit in AMI-CS. Trade-off: composite safety endpoint 24.0% vs 6.2% (bleeding, limb ischemia, device failure, worsening AR) — a real 17.8% absolute increase. 10-year follow-up (ESC 2025): benefit grows — 16.3% absolute mortality reduction, ~600 additional days alive on average.

rows: Mild-moderate shock, bridge while assessing, resource-limited settings. Declining use (44.9% → 32.9%)
STEMI + CS, SCAI C–D — DanGer Shock-proven, NNT 8, ACC/AHA Class 2a. Most CS protocols now default here
SCAI E, refractory shock, arrest, biventricular failure. Highest support, highest complication risk
Persistent shock despite percutaneous MCS, or transplant candidates — bridge to recovery/transplant/durable VAD

items: 1. Recognize shock physiology (SBP < 90 or MAP < 60, lactate > 2, cool extremities, altered mentation) and assign a SCAI stage immediately — it drives every subsequent decision.
2. Identify the etiology fast — STEMI → cath lab now; mechanical complication → echo immediately. Door-to-support time is directly tied to survival.

3. First-line pharmacologic support: norepinephrine first-line; dobutamine if low output without severe hypotension. Don't rely on high-dose vasopressors alone if shock persists past the initial bolus.
4. Escalate to MCS without delay — SCAI C–D with STEMI: Impella CP before or immediately after PCI (door-to-Impella time correlates with outcome).
5. Reassess hourly — rising lactate, worsening SCAI stage, or new organ failure means escalate again; SCAI E or refractory → VA-ECMO + shock-team activation.
6. Plan the exit from day one — daily hemodynamic assessment, lactate clearance, vasopressor wean trial; document recovery vs transplant vs durable VAD pathway.

body.text: Weaning: cardiac index > 2.2, lactate normalized/clearing, vasopressors weaned or minimal; reduce device flow stepwise reassessing q30–60 min; echo for LVEF improvement and no worsening MR/AR before removal. Survivor outcomes: 7.0% 30-day, 24.5% 1-year, 38.9% 3-year mortality; 22% rehospitalized within 30 days, 58% within a year — structured HF follow-up for CS survivors is not optional.
